authors: Wesley M. Cohen; Daniel A. Levinthal
title: Absorptive Capacity: A New Perspective on Learning and Innovation
question: Why does prior related knowledge affect a firm’s ability to benefit from external technological information?
sample: 1,719 business units from 318 firms in 151 lines of business.
design: Cross-sectional linkage of R&D-manager technological-opportunity surveys with FTC Line of Business data.
measures: Business-unit R&D intensity, industry knowledge sources, appropriability and technological opportunity.
results: Patterns of R&D investment were consistent with an absorptive role for internal research.
inference: Indirect empirical assessment of a learning mechanism; not direct causal estimation of absorptive capacity.
competing_explanations: Unobserved innovative opportunity, coarse industry knowledge measures and endogenous R&D investment.
classroom_use: Use to explain why equally available information produces unequal learning and to distinguish access from assimilation.
coverage: Conceptual opening; organizational absorption discussion; Data and Measures pp. 142–143; empirical framework and discussion.

authors: Dennis Epple; Linda Argote; Rukmini Devadas
title: Organizational Learning Curves: A Method for Investigating Intra-Plant Transfer of Knowledge Acquired Through Learning by Doing
question: Is production knowledge fully embodied in equipment, or does some of it remain associated with people and organizational experience?
sample: Production observations from an automobile assembly plant before and after addition of a second shift.
design: Generalized learning-curve estimation with tests of complete carryover, cross-shift transfer and retention restrictions.
measures: Output, labor and production inputs, accumulated experience, shift-specific and shared knowledge parameters.
results: Complete transfer was rejected; substantial knowledge carried over, with incomplete later cross-shift transfer.
inference: A discriminating observational test against complete technological embodiment.
competing_explanations: Model misspecification, workforce differences and contemporaneous production changes.
classroom_use: Use as a concrete test of where organizational knowledge resides, with a clear prediction that could be rejected.
coverage: Abstract p. 58; intra-plant knowledge-transfer model; estimation and discussion pp. 65–70.

title: Core Capabilities and Core Rigidities: A Paradox in Managing New Product Development
question: How can the same core capability support successful development and obstruct a project requiring new knowledge?
sample: Twenty product/process projects across Ford, Chaparral Steel, Hewlett-Packard and two anonymous firms.
design: Comparative qualitative cases; cross-team analysis, interviews, site visits and member checks.
measures: Four capability dimensions and their alignment with project requirements.
results: The same interdependent knowledge system both enables projects and constrains unfamiliar requirements.
inference: Inductive mechanism inference; not a universal causal performance relationship.
competing_explanations: Project differences, retrospective accounts, company participation and mixed definitions of project success.
classroom_use: Use to explain the mechanism behind capability rigidity before presenting later statistical evidence on adaptation and innovation.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: PDF pp. 3–4, framework and project sample; PDF pp. 6–7 and 10–11, selected project evidence; PDF pp. 14 and 16, conclusion and methodology appendix. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: Measuring Competence? Exploring Firm Effects in Pharmaceutical Research
question: Can measured organizational competences explain research productivity beyond firm size, portfolio composition and unexplained firm effects?
sample: Ten major European and U.S. pharmaceutical firms; research-program analysis focused on 1975–1988.
design: Program-level patent-output models combined with qualitative organizational histories.
measures: Research investment, prior patents, portfolio scope, publication incentives and resource-allocation structure.
results: Some architectural practices and prior success associate with output; portfolio and firm effects complicate interpretation.
inference: Associations consistent with competence, explicitly not a convincing separation from all unobserved heterogeneity.
competing_explanations: Scientist quality, scientific opportunities, patent propensity, agency problems and research-portfolio composition.
classroom_use: Use as a canonical attempt to open the firm-effect black box, with its own measurement cautions retained.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: PDF pp. 8–9 (printed pp. 69–70), data; PDF pp. 16–18 (printed pp. 77–79), results and conclusions. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: Knowledge and the Speed of the Transfer and Imitation of Organizational Capabilities: An Empirical Test
question: Do the knowledge characteristics that facilitate internal replication also make a capability easier for competitors to imitate?
sample: 35 major Swedish innovations analyzed; the questionnaire initially targeted 44 innovations associated with 20 firms.
design: Observational analysis of time to capability transfer and product imitation.
measures: Codifiability, teachability, complexity, employee turnover, continuing development and transfer/imitation timing.
results: Knowledge codification and teachability accelerated transfer; imitation effects were qualified and influenced by mobility and continued development.
inference: Evidence links knowledge attributes to transfer hazards without experimentally assigning those attributes.
competing_explanations: Recall error, selected successful innovations, product/manufacturing outcome mismatch and omitted protection mechanisms.
classroom_use: Use to make causal ambiguity and transferability concrete, and to test the simple proposition that anything transferable internally must be equally easy to imitate externally.
coverage: Abstract pp. 76–77; sample pp. 80–81; transfer/imitation results and field illustrations.

title: The Resource-Based View of the Firm in Two Environments: The Hollywood Film Studios from 1936 to 1965
question: When do property-based resources and knowledge-based resources contribute to performance under different environmental conditions?
sample: Seven major Hollywood studios, 1936–1965; RKO excluded because it ceased operations before the end.
design: Historical autoregressive/heteroscedastic regressions separated by era.
measures: Star contracts, theater control, Academy Awards and prior production costs; ROS, profits and share.
results: Property-based resources stronger in stable era; knowledge-based indicators stronger in uncertain era.
inference: Historical conditional association, not an isolated causal effect of uncertainty.
competing_explanations: Other era changes, survival selection, legal change and imperfect archival proxies.
classroom_use: Use as the central empirical illustration that valuable resources must be specified relative to environmental conditions.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: PDF pp. 11–12 and 14 (printed pp. 528–529 and 531), sample and variables; PDF p. 20 (printed p. 537), Tables 4–5; PDF pp. 22–23, discussion. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: Exploring Internal Stickiness: Impediments to the Transfer of Best Practice Within the Firm
question: Why are superior practices difficult to transfer between units that belong to the same firm?
sample: 271 questionnaires concerning 122 transfers of 38 practices across eight companies.
design: Two-stage survey with source, recipient and third-party reports; canonical correlation analysis.
measures: Transfer stickiness by stage; absorptive capacity, causal ambiguity, relational difficulty and motivational barriers.
results: Largest reported barriers were recipient absorption, causal ambiguity and arduous relationships.
inference: Associational comparison of barriers; canonical weights do not yield randomized causal effects.
competing_explanations: Selected transfer histories, respondent recall, measurement overlap and unstable smaller-sample estimates.
classroom_use: Use as core empirical evidence that internal replication remains costly, and as a bridge between sustained advantage and the difficulty of scaling it.
coverage: Abstract/introduction pp. 27–28; transfer stages; Method and sample; Discussion pp. 36–38.

title: SPECIALIZED SUPPLIER NETWORKS AS A SOURCE OF COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE: EVIDENCE FROM THE AUTO INDUSTRY
question: Can specialized relationships between separate firms create competitive advantage, and which partners capture the resulting gains?
sample: Two Japanese and three U.S. automakers plus selected partner and arm’s-length suppliers.
design: Comparative surveys/interviews, descriptive network plots, selected regressions and rank correlations.
measures: Plant proximity; nonredeployable assets; face-to-face contact; quality, inventory, development cycle and ROA.
results: Some specificity dimensions associate with better network performance; physical specificity–quality prediction is unsupported.
inference: Suggestive observational comparisons; five-producer outcomes do not support strong causal claims.
competing_explanations: National institutions, trust, selection of supplier ties, product quality and bargaining/appropriation.
classroom_use: Use to connect value creation through specialization with appropriation and governance, while showing the limits of small-network comparisons.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Sample and data collection; Performance measures and Data analysis; Performance discussion; Conclusion boundary conditions. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: CAPABILITIES, TECHNOLOGICAL DIVERSIFICATION AND DIVISIONALIZATION
question: How is technological diversification related to the internal division structure of a multidivisional firm?
sample: 106 large U.S. multidivisional firms; 1975 structure and 1974–1981 patent information.
design: Cross-sectional OLS models with sector and diversification controls.
measures: Patent technological diversity; divisions/subsidiaries relative to revenues; sector and strategic diversification.
results: Negative diversity–divisionalization association, conditioned by sector’s technological progressiveness.
inference: Associational organization–strategy fit; causal direction is explicitly ambiguous.
competing_explanations: Simultaneity, patenting propensities, size scaling and unobserved internal decision rights.
classroom_use: Use as a bridge from knowledge complementarities to internal organizational design and the limits of highly autonomous divisions.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Empirical methods and measure discussion; Sample/models; results narrative preceding Conclusion. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: AN EMPIRICAL TEST OF THE RESOURCE-BASED THEORY: STRATEGIC REGULATION IN THE DUTCH AUDIT INDUSTRY
question: How can regulation make professional human capital valuable and protect the rents attached to it?
sample: Dutch audit profession in the postwar period; membership histories and selected income years.
design: Historical longitudinal industry analysis; comparisons of regulatory and nonregulatory periods.
measures: Disclosed accounts, qualified employees and partners, concentration, promotions and professional income.
results: Regulation enlarges demand; professional and partnership constraints help protect scarce positions.
inference: Historical and statistical association; no isolated regulatory treatment estimate.
competing_explanations: Secular demand growth, technology/productivity changes and limited income data.
classroom_use: Use to ask where valuable, scarce resources come from and how institutional rules protect or distribute their returns.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Evidence: Hypotheses 1 and 2; Conjectures 1–2 on rent appropriation. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: Know-how and asset complementarity and dynamic capability accumulation: the case of r&d
question: How do existing technological knowledge and complementary physical assets shape investment in new capabilities after an environmental change?
sample: 26 major U.S. energy firms, 1976–1981.
design: Tobit regressions; lagged regressors; alternative lagged-dependent-variable and firm-effect specifications.
measures: Coal-conversion R&D/sales; refining R&D capital; complementary physical assets; oil prices.
results: Related knowledge predicts coal-conversion R&D; some complementary-asset coefficients depend on specification.
inference: Association in capability investment, not causal evidence of performance advantage.
competing_explanations: Oil prices, firm size, firm effects, prior spending and correlated knowledge stocks are considered.
classroom_use: Use to explain where dynamic capabilities come from and why resource complementarities remain contingent on market conditions.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Data; Empirical methodology and variables; Empirical results narrative around Table 7; Conclusion. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: Information technology as competitive advantage: the role of human, business, and technology resources
question: Why do firms using similar information technologies achieve different performance, and can IT alone explain advantage?
sample: 65 retail firms; home-office responses with remote store-manager validation.
design: Cross-sectional resource-performance regressions supplemented by interviews and interrater checks.
measures: Human/business resources, in-store and beyond-store IT, financial and IT performance.
results: Human complements predict performance; IT alone is nonsignificant; business effects are weaker with human resources controlled.
inference: Association only; authors explicitly state sustainability and causal direction are not established.
competing_explanations: Reverse causality, common-method perceptions, industry specificity and technology diffusion.
classroom_use: Use as a concrete case showing that buying a visible resource may not reproduce the organizational system behind successful use.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Data and measures: Sample; Data analysis and findings; Discussion and limitations. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: Relative absorptive capacity and interorganizational learning
question: Why can a firm learn effectively from one partner but struggle to learn from another?
sample: Pharmaceutical–biotechnology R&D alliances with organizational and scientific-knowledge information.
design: Observational alliance study combining bibliometric data and organizational survey measures.
measures: Knowledge-base similarity, structures, compensation, research communities, R&D spending and learning.
results: Selected relative-compatibility measures predicted learning more strongly than R&D spending alone.
inference: Evidence for a relational learning mechanism, subject to partner-selection effects.
competing_explanations: Self-selection of compatible partners, reported learning, prior relationships and unmeasured alliance governance.
classroom_use: Use to explain why access to a valuable partner’s knowledge does not ensure successful learning and why partner matching matters.
coverage: Abstract p. 461; relative absorptive-capacity theory; measures and Results section.

title: SOCIAL CAPITAL AND VALUE CREATION: THE ROLE OF INTRAFIRM NETWORKS.
question: How do social relationships among business units contribute to resource exchange and product innovation?
sample: Fifteen business units of one multinational electronics company; three key respondents sought per unit.
design: Observational multisource network survey and structural-equation/path analysis.
measures: Social interaction, trustworthiness, shared vision, interunit resource exchange and product innovation.
results: Social interaction and trust related to resource exchange, which related to innovation.
inference: Associational support for the proposed mechanism, with weak temporal identification.
competing_explanations: Reverse causality, small unit-level sample, shared organizational setting and correlated respondent perceptions.
classroom_use: Use to connect the organizational-advantage argument to observable relationships, while illustrating the inferential limits of early capability research.
coverage: Introduction p. 464; Methods pp. 468–470; Results and model discussion.

authors: James G. Combs; David J. Ketchen, Jr.
title: Explaining interfirm cooperation and performance: toward a reconciliation of predictions from the resource-based view and organizational economics
question: How do resource needs and exchange conditions jointly explain cooperation choices and subsequent firm performance?
sample: 94 publicly held restaurant chains; archival measures and hospitality-expert assessments.
design: Regression and interaction analyses of cooperation choices and performance, with later-year checks.
measures: Resource availability/reputation/management experience; exchange conditions; cooperation; ROA and market-to-book.
results: Resource and exchange conditions interact; several resource-performance and alignment predictions receive only partial support.
inference: Observational associations; later convergence cannot establish that cooperation built capabilities.
competing_explanations: Scale, growth, firm age, limited construct proxies and alternative subsequent strategic changes.
classroom_use: Use as a direct empirical comparison of RBV and organizational economics, including the costs of prioritizing resource access.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Measures; Results; Discussion of resource/exchange interaction and performance; Limitations. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: The Search-Transfer Problem: The Role of Weak Ties in Sharing Knowledge across Organization Subunits
question: When do weak relationships facilitate knowledge sharing, and when do they become an obstacle?
sample: 120 new-product-development projects in 41 divisions; 54 reported an interdivisional transfer event.
design: Observational network and project study combining surveys and archives.
measures: Interunit tie weakness, knowledge codification/complexity, project characteristics and completion time.
results: Weak ties helped with simpler knowledge but impeded complex transfers; benefits depended on knowledge characteristics.
inference: Conditional associations explaining a search–transfer tradeoff, not experimental tie-strength manipulation.
competing_explanations: Endogenous network formation, project selection, knowledge complexity measurement and single-firm context.
classroom_use: Use to structure the practical question of whether to broaden access or deepen collaboration; the answer depends on the stage and content of knowledge sharing.
coverage: Abstract p. 82; Data and Methods; complexity and tie measures; Discussion pp. 105–106.

title: Localization of Knowledge and the Mobility of Engineers in Regional Networks
question: Why are knowledge spillovers localized in some regions more strongly than in others?
sample: Important semiconductor patents from 1980 and 1985 in twelve major US regions; corresponding citations and inventor mobility.
design: Matched patent-citation comparisons and observational analysis of regional mobility.
measures: Geographic localization of citations, technological controls and movement of major patent holders across employers.
results: Localization varied across regions; engineer mobility influenced local knowledge flows.
inference: Evidence supports a regional labor-network mechanism without a randomized mobility shock.
competing_explanations: Technology clustering, inventor selection, unobserved regional institutions and citation conventions.
classroom_use: Use to qualify any claim that useful knowledge is naturally contained inside legal firm boundaries.
coverage: Abstract p. 905; patent sampling and geographic controls pp. 908–911; mobility analysis and conclusions.

title: Organizational Routines as a Source of Continuous Change
question: How can repeated organizational routines generate ongoing change through their own performance?
sample: Five routines in a student-housing organization at a large state university, observed for four years.
design: Longitudinal qualitative fieldwork and process comparison across repeated routine performances.
measures: Observations of work and meetings, participant interpretations, expected outcomes and subsequent changes.
results: Participants revised routines in response to failures, unintended outcomes and opportunities.
inference: Evidence identifies plausible within-routine mechanisms rather than a population causal effect.
competing_explanations: Researcher interpretation, setting-specific administrative conditions and concurrent organizational changes.
classroom_use: Use as a challenge to treating routines solely as inertia and as a concrete example before introducing dynamic capabilities.
coverage: Abstract; methods and organizational context; descriptions of five routines; performative model and discussion.

title: Beyond local search: boundary‐spanning, exploration, and impact in the optical disk industry
question: How do crossing organizational boundaries and crossing technological boundaries differ in their consequences for inventive impact?
sample: Optical-disk patenting firms; 371 firm-year observations reported in the regression tables.
design: Negative-binomial regressions with firm and year controls.
measures: Backward citations classified by organizational/technological boundary; later within-domain and outside-domain citations.
results: Organizational boundary spanning predicts greater impact; technological spanning involves domain-dependent tradeoffs.
inference: Associational evidence on patented inventions, not direct identification of capability-building routines.
competing_explanations: Patent selection, knowledge quality, patent age and the selection of external technologies matter.
classroom_use: Use as empirical evidence that the value of knowledge recombination depends on which boundary is crossed and which outcome is evaluated.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Methodology: Data; Exploration; Impact; Results narrative; Discussion; Conclusions. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

authors: Andrew A. King; Christopher L. Tucci
title: Incumbent Entry into New Market Niches: The Role of Experience and Managerial Choice in the Creation of Dynamic Capabilities
question: Does experience in established markets hinder entry into new technological niches, or equip incumbents to enter successfully?
sample: 208 business units representing 174 organizations in rigid disk drives, 1976–1995.
design: Random-effects logistic entry models; Heckman-style selection correction for future sales.
measures: Production/sales experience, prior niche transitions, entry and subsequent sales.
results: Existing-market experience favors entry; prior-transition effect is not positive as hypothesized.
inference: Observational entry and performance evidence; managerial choice mechanism inferred.
competing_explanations: Industry transition speed, incumbent selection, prior market position and sampling differences discussed.
classroom_use: Pair with rigidity cases to distinguish average incumbent advantages from the failures of particular market leaders.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Research method and Sample; Results opening paragraphs; Discussion; Conclusions. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: The dynamics of product innovation and firm competences
question: How does developing a new product both draw on existing competences and build competences for future activity?
sample: Five high-technology firms producing physical business-to-business products.
design: Comparative qualitative field study using interviews, observations and documents.
measures: Technological/customer competence, product projects and competence development traced qualitatively.
results: Product innovation both deploys and develops competences; exploiting technology requires complementary customer competences.
inference: Inductive mechanism account; no population effect estimate.
competing_explanations: Case selection, retrospective interpretation and simultaneous changes in markets/resources.
classroom_use: Use to make the resource-services distinction tangible through product development and to introduce first- versus second-order competences.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Methods opening; Discussion and managerial/limitations sections, selected excerpts. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

authors: Michael J. Leiblein; Jeffrey J. Reuer; Frédéric Dalsace
title: Do make or buy decisions matter? The influence of organizational governance on technological performance
question: Does producing internally rather than outsourcing improve technological performance, once firms’ selection of governance is considered?
sample: 714 semiconductor product-market/process-technology production decisions from 1996 industry information.
design: Two-stage governance-choice and technological-performance models with selection correction.
measures: Make/buy, exchange hazards, governance misfit and standardized feature size.
results: Direct governance effect is nonsignificant after correction; inadequate safeguards associate with lower technological performance.
inference: Modeled observational comparison; selection assumptions remain essential.
competing_explanations: Capability-driven selection, systemic coordination demands, transaction hazards and omitted attributes.
classroom_use: Use to compare capability selection with TCE alignment, and to explain why a raw make-versus-buy performance comparison is inadequate.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Methodology: Data and technological-performance measure; Second-stage results opening; Discussion. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: Knowledge Networks: Explaining Effective Knowledge Sharing in Multiunit Companies
question: Why do some units obtain useful knowledge from the rest of a diversified firm while others fail to realize that potential?
sample: 120 new-product-development projects in 41 units of a multinational electronics company.
design: Observational project/network study combining competency classifications and surveys.
measures: Related knowledge, network-path length, direct ties, knowledge obtained, codifiability and completion time.
results: Benefits required related knowledge accessible through short paths; direct ties had contingent effects by codification.
inference: Evidence for content–network complementarity, not a randomized test of organizational links.
competing_explanations: Network endogeneity, recall and single-company context; shared setting with earlier Hansen studies.
classroom_use: Use to explain why corporate relatedness alone cannot guarantee synergy and why integration requires particular lateral connections.
coverage: Abstract p. 232; Data and Methods pp. 236–238; knowledge-network definitions and results.

authors: Prashant Kale; Jeffrey H. Dyer; Harbir Singh
title: Alliance capability, stock market response, and long‐term alliance success: the role of the alliance function
question: Does alliance experience improve alliance success by itself, or through dedicated structures that capture and apply what firms learn?
sample: Firms and their alliances formed during 1993–1997; primary and alliance-level respondents plus stock-market data.
design: Survey/event-study regressions and Heckman selection models.
measures: Dedicated alliance function, alliance experience, abnormal returns, multidimensional managerial success assessments.
results: Alliance function remains a predictor; the independent experience effect diminishes with selection correction.
inference: Associational triangulation with a modeled selection correction, not random adoption of structures.
competing_explanations: Learning orientation, self-selection, partner quality, signaling, and organizational placement.
classroom_use: Use to explain how firms organize learning rather than treating repetition as an automatic capability-building process.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Research design and variable definitions; Discussion; Limitations and future research. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

authors: Roger G. Schroeder; Kimberly A. Bates; Mikko A. Junttila
title: A resource‐based view of manufacturing strategy and the relationship to manufacturing performance
question: How do learning practices become difficult-to-copy manufacturing resources associated with plant performance?
sample: 164 plants in Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States; three manufacturing industries.
design: Cross-sectional multiple-respondent survey and structural-equation modeling.
measures: Internal/external learning, proprietary processes/equipment and manufacturing performance.
results: Learning–proprietary process and proprietary process–performance paths are positive; original model fit is imperfect.
inference: Associational pathway; temporal mediation and sustained advantage are untested.
competing_explanations: Construct coverage, reverse causality, country/industry differences and post hoc model modifications.
classroom_use: Use to make the learning-to-resource-to-performance chain concrete while distinguishing a fitted mediation model from causal process evidence.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Description of data and measures; Test of hypotheses, including model-fit and limitations paragraphs. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: Social Structure of “Coopetition” Within a Multiunit Organization: Coordination, Competition, and Intraorganizational Knowledge Sharing
question: How do formal coordination and informal relationships affect knowledge sharing when business units also compete with one another?
sample: Twenty-four business units in one large diversified petrochemical-origin company.
design: Observational sociometric analysis of interunit networks and competition.
measures: Knowledge sharing, centralization, social interaction, market competition and internal-resource competition.
results: Centralization related negatively to sharing; social interaction benefits depended on competition type.
inference: Conditional within-firm association rather than causal proof that decentralization improves sharing.
competing_explanations: Endogenous structure, previous sharing, unit status and unobserved interdependencies.
classroom_use: Use to challenge the simple assumption that hierarchy automatically integrates knowledge, and to connect agency and internal power concerns with KBV.
coverage: Abstract p. 179; Methods pp. 183–185; coordination measures and results.

authors: Michael J. Leiblein; Douglas J. Miller
title: An empirical examination of transaction‐ and firm‐level influences on the vertical boundaries of the firm
question: Can transaction attributes and firm-specific experience jointly explain where firms draw vertical boundaries?
sample: 469 make/buy production decisions from 117 responding semiconductor manufacturers.
design: Binary governance-choice models; alternative experience specifications including instrumentalized variables.
measures: Fabrication and sourcing experience, diversification, specificity, uncertainty and supplier availability.
results: Both firm-level experience and transaction attributes explain choices; specificity works conditionally with uncertainty.
inference: Associations in endogenous boundary choice, not causal performance estimates.
competing_explanations: Prior choices generating experience, size, tenure, market strategy, geography and supplier availability.
classroom_use: Use as direct evidence for combining capability differences with TCE rather than holding firm capabilities constant.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Research design: Sample and specification; Results opening; Discussion. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: Network Structure and Knowledge Transfer: The Effects of Cohesion and Range
question: Do network structure and knowledge diversity affect transfer beyond the strength of the direct relationship between sender and receiver?
sample: Employees of one contract R&D firm; 104 of 113 employees returned the survey.
design: Observational network analysis combining survey, expertise and personnel information.
measures: Ease of knowledge transfer, cohesion, range, tie strength, expertise overlap and codifiability.
results: Cohesion and range eased reported transfer after accounting for direct tie strength.
inference: Conditional associations support distinct mechanisms but do not establish exogenous network effects.
competing_explanations: Shared-source response bias, homophily, selection into ties and prior successful cooperation.
classroom_use: Use alongside Hansen to show why the weak-tie/strong-tie distinction alone does not capture the full social architecture of transfer.
coverage: Abstract p. 240; methods pp. 248–252; results and discussion.

authors: Gautam Ray; Jay B. Barney; Waleed A. Muhanna
title: Capabilities, business processes, and competitive advantage: choosing the dependent variable in empirical tests of the resource‐based view
question: At what level should researchers measure performance when testing whether resources produce competitive advantages?
sample: 104 North American life and health insurance firms responding from an 800-firm sampling frame.
design: Multi-informant survey; structural-equation models of process and firm outcomes.
measures: Service climate, managerial IT knowledge, technology scope, spending, customer service and ROA.
results: Intangible capabilities predict some process outcomes but not ROA; technology/spending measures are nonsignificant.
inference: Outcome-level association, not a test identifying rent recipients.
competing_explanations: Other business-process disadvantages, appropriation, respondent perceptions and sample selection.
classroom_use: Use to compare process effectiveness, competitive advantage and accounting returns before pooling empirical support for RBV.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Data and method: Sample; Independent and dependent variable measures; Results; Disaggregating firm performance; Resource-based logic and business processes. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

authors: Kyle J. Mayer; Nicholas S. Argyres
title: Learning to Contract: Evidence from the Personal Computer Industry
question: How do firms learn to write contracts, and what knowledge do contracts preserve as a relationship develops?
sample: Softstar and several customers; eleven focal contracts with HW Inc., 1989–1997.
design: Contract-history case study and repeated interviews with managers and technical personnel.
measures: Changes in contract terms following experienced coordination and project problems.
results: Contracts evolve through problem-driven learning and preserve collaboration knowledge; transfer across customer relationships is limited.
inference: Qualitative process inference with source triangulation; no estimated population effect.
competing_explanations: Anticipatory TCE explanations, relationship-specific learning, resource limits and retrospective interpretation.
classroom_use: Use to integrate contracting and learning theories through observable contract revisions, and to explain the development of governance capabilities.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Methods and setting; Learning to contract interpretation; Conclusion. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

authors: Martine R. Haas; Morten T. Hansen
title: When using knowledge can hurt performance: the value of organizational capabilities in a management consulting company
question: Can using a firm’s accumulated knowledge resources reduce rather than improve competitive task performance?
sample: 182 sales proposals in one large US management consulting company.
design: Observational survey and archival study informed by interviews; models of contract wins.
measures: Use of electronic documents and personal advice, team experience, differentiation requirements and contracts won.
results: Knowledge use could hurt experienced teams; document reuse could hurt teams needing differentiation.
inference: Conditional association, not randomized access or an exogenous knowledge-sharing intervention.
competing_explanations: Task difficulty, endogenous consultation, unobserved team quality and proposal selection.
classroom_use: Use as an explicit negative or contingent result against the blanket claim that more knowledge sharing always improves performance.
coverage: Abstract p. 1; research setting and sampling; contract-won and knowledge-use measures; results and conclusion.

authors: Morten T. Hansen; Marie Louise Mors; Bjørn Løvås
title: Knowledge Sharing in Organizations: Multiple Networks, Multiple Phases
question: Do the same social-network conditions help all stages of knowledge sharing?
sample: 121 teams in 41 subsidiaries; search-cost analysis 55 projects and transfer-cost analysis 50.
design: Observational multilevel network study with phase-specific outcomes and clustered inference.
measures: Team density, interunit network size, tie strength, perceived competition, search decisions and search/transfer costs.
results: Network effects differed by phase; competition raised costs; strong transfer ties helped with tacit knowledge.
inference: Mechanism-consistent associations; subsets require selection caution.
competing_explanations: Endogenous networks, selection into search/transfer, single-company setting and overlap with earlier research context.
classroom_use: Use to build a staged process explanation instead of treating knowledge sharing as one variable with one set of determinants.
coverage: Abstract p. 776; Methods and Data; Results; Discussion and Conclusion.

authors: Sendil K. Ethiraj; Prashant Kale; M. S. Krishnan; Jitendra V. Singh
title: Where do capabilities come from and how do they matter? A study in the software services industry
question: Where do operational capabilities arise, and how do they contribute to profitability at the level of individual projects?
sample: 138 projects for 57 clients at one Indian software-services firm, 1996–2001.
design: Project-level panel models with client fixed effects; GLS alternatives.
measures: Project contribution; new/repeat client; schedule slippage; effort overrun; process defects.
results: Two project-management measures predict contribution; client-specific effect is specification-sensitive.
inference: Within-client associations, not an experimentally isolated investment return.
competing_explanations: Unobserved client heterogeneity, coarse experience measures, project complexity and overlap between costs/outcomes.
classroom_use: Use for operationalizing capabilities and teaching why mixed or specification-sensitive results belong in an evidence review.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Methods: Data and model specification; Results narrative; Discussion paragraphs on client effects and project management. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: Presumptive adaptation and the effectiveness of knowledge transfer
question: When does adapting a transferred organizational practice undermine the benefits of knowledge transfer?
sample: Cross-border development of the Mail Boxes Etc. franchise network in Israel.
design: In-depth longitudinal field investigation using interviews and reconstruction of practice adoption and network development.
measures: Adherence to recommended franchising practices and new-franchise/network growth.
results: Presumptive adaptation accompanied stalled growth; closer adherence accompanied rapid expansion.
inference: Process evidence consistent with a diagnostic-template mechanism; no randomized assignment.
competing_explanations: Changes in management, market conditions, resources or franchisee composition could also affect growth.
classroom_use: Use as process evidence for replication theory and as a counterweight to the intuitive claim that immediate local adaptation always improves fit.
coverage: Abstract p. 937; field setting and methods; adherence measures; network-growth analysis and concluding discussion.

authors: Jeffrey H. Dyer; Nile W. Hatch
title: Relation‐specific capabilities and barriers to knowledge transfers: creating advantage through network relationships
question: Can buyers obtain different performance from the same suppliers, and why does shared supplier knowledge not automatically erase the difference?
sample: 42 U.S. supplier plants serving both Toyota and a major U.S. automaker; retrospective 1990–1996 comparisons.
design: Matched within-supplier quantitative comparisons plus exploratory interviews.
measures: Knowledge-sharing activity/assistance; defects and inventories for matched customer operations.
results: Toyota operations improve more; network constraints and internal rigidities impede reuse for other customers.
inference: Matched observational evidence plus qualitative mechanisms; not randomized transfer assistance.
competing_explanations: Customer-specific processes, contract timing, volume differences and targeted help to weaker suppliers.
classroom_use: Use to explain relational capability and why knowledge transfer across firms can coexist with barriers to transfer within a supplier.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Research methods: Sample and measures; Results opening; Conclusion. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: Technological Development and the Boundaries of the Firm: A Knowledge-Based Examination in Semiconductor Manufacturing
question: When do integrated or specialized semiconductor manufacturers solve technological development problems more effectively?
sample: Semiconductor manufacturing facilities: 36 facilities from 32 firms in collected data; analysis restricted to 1995–2001.
design: Comparative observational models of technological-development performance across integrated and specialized manufacturers.
measures: Development time, initial yield, problem structure and complexity, scale and scope measures.
results: Specialists were faster even as complexity increased; integrated producers had quality advantages on complex problems.
inference: Qualified evidence for organizational matching; results depend on performance dimension.
competing_explanations: Endogenous organization and problem selection, capability differences and economies of scale or scope.
classroom_use: Use as a substantive empirical qualification of KBV predictions, emphasizing that coordination can affect speed and quality differently.
coverage: Abstract p. 826; data and measures; results Tables 4–5 and discussion pp. 839–841.

authors: Frank T. Rothaermel; Andrew M. Hess
title: Building Dynamic Capabilities: Innovation Driven by Individual-, Firm-, and Network-Level Effects
question: How do people, internal R&D and external alliances jointly contribute to an incumbent’s innovation under technological change?
sample: 81 incumbent pharmaceutical firms followed from 1980–2001 after reconstructing predecessor/merger histories.
design: Longitudinal patent-output models with multilevel predictors and interaction tests.
measures: Scientists/stars/nonstars, R&D, biotech alliances, granted biotech patent applications.
results: Star effect is conditional on nonstar controls; human capital substitutes for some inputs; R&D and alliances complement.
inference: Associational multilevel evidence; interactions are not independently manipulated mechanisms.
competing_explanations: Unobserved innovation strategy, firm scale, prior patents, merger histories and selection of scientists/alliances.
classroom_use: Use to challenge both a star-employee-only account and the assumption that all useful resources are mutually complementary.

authors: Martine R. Haas; Morten T. Hansen
title: Different knowledge, different benefits: toward a productivity perspective on knowledge sharing in organizations
question: Do codified documents and personal advice produce the same benefits for knowledge-intensive work?
sample: 182 sales teams in a large US management consulting company.
design: Observational team survey, with interviews informing measurement and regressions by task outcome.
measures: Document use, advice, time saved, work quality, competence signaling, document rework and advisor effort.
results: Codified and personal knowledge delivered different benefits; process costs reduced outcomes.
inference: Differentiated correlations support mechanisms, not randomized comparisons of knowledge forms.
competing_explanations: Self-reported outcomes, endogenous knowledge use, correlated task difficulty and reused empirical context.
classroom_use: Use to replace an undifferentiated knowledge-performance arrow with a concrete map from knowledge form to specific benefit and cost.
coverage: Abstract p. 1133; Data and Methods pp. 1141–1144; Results and discussion.

title: Does Transaction Misalignment Matter for Firm Survival at All Stages of the Industry Life Cycle?
question: Do inefficiently aligned transactions threaten survival equally at every stage of an industry’s evolution?
sample: Historical population of U.S. automobile producers observed during 1917–1933.
design: Gompertz survival models with engine-governance misalignment and industry-stage interactions.
measures: Engine uniqueness, integration/outsourcing, shakeout period and firm failure.
results: Misalignment is not significant overall but has a mortality penalty during shakeout.
inference: Historical conditional associations, not direct observation of governance costs.
competing_explanations: Scale economies, supplier capabilities, inherited commitments and changing competitive intensity.
classroom_use: Use to compare TCE efficiency predictions with evolutionary selection, including when an inefficient firm can survive.

authors: Deepak Somaya; Ian O. Williamson; Natalia Lorinkova
title: Gone but Not Lost: The Different Performance Impacts of Employee Mobility Between Cooperators Versus Competitors
question: When can losing employees preserve or improve business relationships instead of simply depleting valuable human capital?
sample: 123 patent law firms and 109 corporate potential clients, 1991–1995.
design: Law-firm/client dyad fixed-effects Poisson models with lagged predictors and year effects.
measures: Attorney inflows/outflows by destination; volume of patent work assigned by each client.
results: Client-bound departures associate with business gains; competitor-bound departures associate with losses.
inference: Within-dyad observational association; external-social-capital mechanism remains inferred.
competing_explanations: Client selection, anticipatory hiring, attorney quality, knowledge fit and relationship changes.

title: Organizational antecedents of second‐order competences
question: Which organizational conditions help firms develop the ability to build new technological and marketing competences?
sample: 145 U.S. manufacturing-firm responses in 2000; surviving/responding firms followed in 2004.
design: Two-wave panel and cross-sectional regressions; reverse-direction and performance-control checks.
measures: Second-order marketing/R&D competences; scanning, slack, conflict, cannibalization and failure tolerance.
results: Effects are differentiated; failure tolerance lacks expected support and is negative for lagged R&D competence.
inference: Temporal associations and reverse-direction tests, not randomized organizational interventions.
competing_explanations: Selective attrition, informant changes, unmeasured antecedents and weak longitudinal marketing prediction.
classroom_use: Use to answer the antecedents question empirically and show why familiar prescriptions for innovation need qualified evidence.
coverage: Selected source excerpts: Data collection; Findings opening; Reverse-causation tests; Discussion on organizational antecedents. Tables and other sections not fully reviewed.

title: Value, rareness, competitive advantage, and performance: a conceptual‐level empirical investigation of the resource‐based view of the firm
question: Can the central RBV concepts of value and rarity be measured and linked separately to advantage and performance?
sample: Micro- and nanotechnology firms; 117 returned surveys, with analysis-specific missing-data reductions.
design: Cross-sectional hierarchical OLS and mediation tests across resource categories.
measures: Perceived value, rarity, competitive advantage and performance.
results: Value/rarity generally predict advantage; rarity mediation partly supported; value mediation unsupported.
inference: Associational conceptual-level test, not proof of causal or sustained advantage.
competing_explanations: Common respondent bias, construct overlap, subjective shadow values and emerging-market demand uncertainty.
classroom_use: Use beside RBV critiques to show an explicit operationalization attempt and the specific predictions that remain unsupported.

authors: David G. Sirmon; Michael A. Hitt
title: Contingencies within dynamic managerial capabilities: interdependent effects of resource investment and deployment on firm performance
question: When does investing more or less than rivals create value, and how does resource deployment change that relationship?
sample: 284 U.S. regional banks; 1,119 firm-year observations, 1998–2002.
design: Panel analysis of investment deviations and investment–deployment interactions.
measures: Human/physical capital investment relative to rivals; service sophistication; Tobin’s q.
results: Investment deviation alone is unfavorable; deployment fit matters with one predicted low-investment combination unsupported.
inference: Observational conditional relationships; managerial capability inferred from decisions.
competing_explanations: Industry recipes, market selection, resource-quality proxies and omitted strategic differences.

authors: Jamal Shamsie; Xavier Martin; Danny Miller
title: In with the old, in with the new: capabilities, strategies, and performance among the Hollywood studios
question: When should project-based firms repeat established strengths, and when should they build capabilities in new project categories?
sample: Seven major Hollywood studios, 7,124 films, 1936–1965.
design: Historical studio-level regression analysis with strategy–resource and strategy–demand interactions.
measures: Genre replication/renewal relative to own and rivals’ success; theaters, stars, demand; ROS with ROA checks.
results: Differentiated strategies perform better; resource and demand conditions alter their payoffs.
inference: Conditional observational associations; genre allocation is a proxy for capability development.
competing_explanations: Reverse performance feedback, genre-demand shifts, resource access and historical-industry specificity.
classroom_use: Use to connect replication and renewal to concrete competitive alternatives rather than assuming that more change always improves performance.

title: Technology, Identity, and Inertia Through the Lens of “The Digital Photography Company”
question: Why can an organization resist a technological opportunity even when it possesses relevant technical competences?
sample: Linco, 1996–2006, including interviews and participant observation during portions of its life.
design: Inductive longitudinal case study with internal and external archival triangulation.
measures: Identity claims, routines, product decisions and reactions to technological opportunities.
results: Identity-challenging opportunities face attention/action barriers; identity change is slow and systemically embedded.
inference: Qualitative process theory; one case does not establish general effect prevalence.
competing_explanations: Technological uncertainty, financial pressures, leadership change and researcher participation.
classroom_use: Use beside resource-cognition and capability-rigidity readings to explain why technical feasibility does not settle adaptation.

title: Trying to become a different type of company: dynamic capability at Smith Corona
question: Why can a firm actively attempt renewal yet fail to redeploy its resources into viable new products?
sample: Smith Corona, 1980–2001; archives and 17 executive/director interviews.
design: Historical extended case method with triangulation and member checks.
measures: Resource alterations and managerial resource schemas reconstructed from decisions and accounts.
results: Renewal attempts failed; beliefs about brand fungibility shaped unproductive paths.
inference: Qualitative mechanism explanation, not an isolated causal effect or universal failure model.
competing_explanations: Retrospective rationalization, industry decline and alternative unrealized resource applications.
classroom_use: Use as a detailed failure case that separates attempted reconfiguration, managerial interpretation and successful adaptation.

authors: Paul L. Drnevich; Aldas P. Kriauciunas
title: Clarifying the conditions and limits of the contributions of ordinary and dynamic capabilities to relative firm performance
question: Do ordinary and dynamic capabilities improve both process outcomes and firm profitability under the same conditions?
sample: 48 Chilean firms reporting 192 business-process changes.
design: Multi-specialist retrospective survey and process-/firm-level regressions.
measures: IT use for existing versus new activities, perceived environmental change, capability heterogeneity, relative performance.
results: Ordinary capabilities positive at both levels; dynamic capability result differs across levels; moderation predictions only partly supported.
inference: Associational evidence; the study discusses reverse causality and delayed returns.
competing_explanations: Poor prior performance prompting change, costs/delays of adjustment, low response and imperfect dynamism measurement.
classroom_use: Use as mixed evidence against treating dynamic capabilities as automatically beneficial, while emphasizing outcome levels and adjustment periods.

authors: Benjamin A. Campbell; Martin Ganco; April M. Franco; Rajshree Agarwal
title: Who leaves, where to, and why worry? employee mobility, entrepreneurship and effects on source firm performance
question: Which employees leave, where do they go, and how do different destinations affect the originating firm?
sample: Linked legal-services employer/employee records in ten U.S. states; restricted to eligible continuing firms and workers.
design: Longitudinal worker mobility and source-firm performance models with robustness checks.
measures: Earnings; established-firm versus spin-out destination; compensation-based revenue-per-employee proxy.
results: Spin-out moves have stronger adverse source-firm associations; destination patterns differ with earnings.
inference: Observational mobility evidence; complementary-asset transfer is an interpreted mechanism.
competing_explanations: Employee quality, involuntary tournament exits, unobserved opportunities, client transfer and earnings measurement.
classroom_use: Use to explain why human capital creates value but cannot be treated as an asset the employer simply owns.

title: Knowledge Inheritance, Vertical Integration, and Entrant Survival in the Early U.S. Auto Industry
question: How does founders’ inherited knowledge shape entrants’ vertical boundaries, strategic positions and survival?
sample: 63 entrants with sufficient data out of 71 identified U.S. auto entrants, 1917–1931.
design: Historical integration, positioning and survival models supplemented with qualitative entrant histories.
measures: Parent engine production, entrant engine integration, strategic positioning and survival.
results: Relevant knowledge inheritance predicts integration; integration supports the differentiation pathway associated with survival.
inference: Historical mechanism-consistent associations, not random inheritance of capabilities.
competing_explanations: Founder pre-employment expertise, entrant selection, transaction hazards and small-sample uncertainty.
classroom_use: Use to show an antecedent of capability heterogeneity and trace how inherited knowledge becomes a consequential organizational choice.

authors: Stéphane J. G. Girod; Richard Whittington
title: Reconfiguration, restructuring and firm performance: Dynamic capabilities and environmental dynamism
question: How do limited organizational reconfigurations and pervasive restructurings differ in their performance consequences?
sample: Top 50 publicly listed industrial Fortune 500 firms in 1985, tracked to 2004; acquisitions reduce later coverage.
design: Archival event coding and dynamic panel System-GMM models.
measures: Restructurings, unit reconfigurations, environmental dynamism, Tobin’s Q and ROA.
results: General restructuring benefit and reconfiguration penalty reverse under high dynamism.
inference: Conditional observational estimates; instrument and coding assumptions matter.
competing_explanations: Performance-triggered reorganization, structural measurement, adjustment lags and large-firm selection.

title: Managing Technological Transitions by Building Bridges
question: When does old technological knowledge help or hinder invention in a new technological generation?
sample: 14 research-active photography incumbents; patents gathered 1974–2010, outcome analysis ending 2004 to allow citation accumulation.
design: Longitudinal Poisson invention-impact models with firm/year controls and interaction tests.
measures: Inventor bridges, analog citations in digital patents, hybrid cameras, analog capability and forward citations.
results: Bridge effects vary by type and prior capability; digital-inventor additions alone are nonsignificant.
inference: Observational inventive-impact associations, not direct causal tests of beliefs or commercial success.
competing_explanations: Patent selection, inventor-history imputation, prior capability and endogeneity of transition choices.
classroom_use: Use to compare persistence and renewal without assuming all old knowledge is either obsolete or automatically useful.

title: Start-up Inertia versus Flexibility: The Role of Founder Identity in a Nascent Industry
question: Why do some young firms remain inert while other start-ups adapt in the same uncertain emerging market?
sample: Four early air-taxi firms; archival coverage 1999–2009 with founder/executive and industry interviews.
design: Inductive comparative longitudinal case study.
measures: Founder identity, venture commitments, experiments, audience expectations and adaptation.
results: Revolutionary/discoverer identity patterns correspond to inertia/flexibility across the cases.
inference: Qualitative theory development; alternative background mechanisms remain possible.
competing_explanations: Funding, founder experience, technology choices and depth of technical expertise examined.
classroom_use: Use as a boundary case against equating youth with flexibility or organizational age with rigidity.

authors: George Chondrakis; Eduardo Melero; Mari Sako
title: The effect of coordination requirements on sourcing decisions: Evidence from patent prosecution services
question: Do increases in coordination requirements cause firms to bring professional services inside, and does prior plural sourcing facilitate adjustment?
sample: 217,480 patent applications, 101 firms, 413 patent classes; applications filed 1995–2005.
design: Difference-in-differences analysis of AIPA, with continuous exposure based on pre-reform patent-class grant lags, firm/class/year effects and heterogeneity by prior plural sourcing.
measures: In-house versus external attorney, pre-reform class grant lag, post-reform period and plural sourcing.
results: Coordination increases encouraged insourcing; response was stronger among prior plural sourcers.
inference: Plausibly causal under exposure and counterfactual-trend assumptions, stronger than a simple cross-sectional correlation.
competing_explanations: Other reform effects correlated with patent-class delays; unobserved differences in adjustment capacity; bundled integration mechanisms.
classroom_use: Use as comparatively strong governance evidence and as an example of why preexisting capabilities affect responses to changes in transaction conditions.
coverage: Title page (2021 online, 2022 issue); Methods and Data pp. 1149–1152; identification and results; conclusion p. 1166.
